reading.passageTitle: Reading Passage 1: Lights on the Coast
paragraphs: A. For more than two thousand years, lighthouses have guided ships along dangerous coasts. The most famous ancient example, the Pharos of Alexandria in Egypt, was completed in the third century BC and is thought to have stood over one hundred metres tall. Early lighthouses relied on open fires burning wood or coal at the top of a tower, but the light they gave was weak and the smoke often blackened the windows of later enclosed lanterns.

B. Building lighthouses on exposed rocks was one of the great engineering challenges of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The Eddystone Rocks off the south-west coast of England saw four lighthouses in less than a century. The first was destroyed by a storm in 1703, and the second by fire. The third, completed by John Smeaton in 1759, used interlocking blocks of granite cut so that each piece fitted tightly into its neighbours, a technique that influenced lighthouse construction for generations.

C. Improvements in the light itself were equally important. In the 1780s, oil lamps with circular wicks produced a brighter, cleaner flame, and curved mirrors were placed behind them to direct the light out to sea. The decisive advance came in 1822, when the French physicist Augustin Fresnel designed a lens made of concentric rings of glass. It was far thinner and lighter than a conventional lens of the same size, and it could bend most of the light into a single powerful beam visible over thirty kilometres away.

D. Each lighthouse needed to be identified by sailors at night. To make this possible, lights were given individual patterns: some flashed at fixed intervals, others showed a steady light interrupted by periods of darkness, and some used coloured glass. These patterns were published in lists so that a navigator who saw a light could work out exactly where the ship was. In fog, when lights could not be seen, many stations used horns, bells or sirens instead.

E. The life of a lighthouse keeper was often lonely and demanding. Keepers had to clean the lens, trim the wicks and keep the light burning through every night, sometimes for weeks without leaving a rock in the middle of the sea. On remote stations, supplies arrived by boat when the weather allowed, and families occasionally lived in the towers or in cottages nearby. Some keepers kept detailed diaries, which are now valuable records of weather and shipping in the past.

F. During the twentieth century, electricity replaced oil, and automatic equipment made resident keepers unnecessary. Most lighthouses in Britain had been automated by the end of the 1990s. Satellite navigation has since reduced the importance of lighthouses for large ships, but many are still maintained as a backup and for smaller boats. Others have been converted into museums, holiday accommodation or bird observatories, preserving buildings that have become symbols of the coast.

A. Desert locusts are usually solitary insects that live quietly in the dry regions stretching from West Africa to India. Most of the time they avoid one another and cause little damage. However, after periods of heavy rain, when vegetation grows quickly and locust numbers rise, a remarkable transformation can take place. As the insects are crowded together, they change their colour, behaviour and even body shape, and begin to move in groups.

B. Researchers have found that the change is triggered partly by touch. When locusts are packed closely, repeated contact on the hind legs causes a rise in the chemical serotonin in their nervous system, which makes them attracted to each other rather than repelled. Within a few hours, a solitary locust can begin to behave like a gregarious one. Over several generations, the gregarious form becomes fully developed, with brighter colours and stronger flight muscles.

C. Once they have formed swarms, locusts can travel great distances with the wind, often covering more than one hundred kilometres a day. A large swarm may contain tens of billions of insects and cover hundreds of square kilometres. Each locust can eat roughly its own weight in fresh food every day, so a swarm can destroy crops that would have fed thousands of people. In 2019 and 2020, swarms in East Africa were the worst seen in decades in some countries.

D. Control has traditionally relied on spraying chemical pesticides, often from aircraft. This can be effective, but it is expensive, it may harm other insects, birds and fish, and it must be carried out quickly in remote areas. Increasingly, organisations favour early action: monitoring the areas where locusts breed and treating small groups before they can form swarms. Satellite data on rainfall and vegetation now help to predict where outbreaks are likely to begin.

E. Biological methods offer an alternative. One product contains spores of a fungus that infects and kills locusts but does not harm most other animals. It works more slowly than chemical pesticides, taking several days to have an effect, which makes it most suitable for treating young locusts before they can fly. Its safety has made it attractive for use in sensitive areas such as farms that produce food for export.

F. Locust swarms are not only a problem; in some places they are also food. Locusts are rich in protein, and they have been eaten in parts of Africa and the Middle East for centuries. Some researchers have suggested that collecting swarming locusts could provide both food and animal feed, although pesticides used in control campaigns can make them unsafe to eat.

A. For much of the twentieth century, many parents and teachers believed that learning two languages in early childhood would confuse children and slow their development. Some early studies seemed to support this view, finding that bilingual children scored lower on intelligence tests. Later researchers pointed out serious weaknesses in these studies: the bilingual children were often from poorer families and were frequently tested in a language they did not know well.

B. In 1962, a study in Montreal by Elizabeth Peal and Wallace Lambert produced very different results. Comparing children from similar backgrounds, they found that bilingual children performed better on a range of tests, especially those requiring flexible thinking. Their work encouraged a new wave of research, and over the following decades, the idea of a bilingual advantage became widely accepted.

C. The explanation most often proposed concerns control of attention. Research shows that in bilingual people both languages are active in the brain at the same time, even when only one is being used. To speak in the right language, a bilingual person must constantly suppress the other one. Some psychologists argued that this daily practice strengthens general mental abilities, such as switching between tasks and ignoring distractions.

D. Studies of older adults added further interest. Research carried out in Canada in the 2000s reported that bilingual patients developed the symptoms of dementia several years later, on average, than monolingual patients with similar levels of education. The researchers did not claim that bilingualism prevents the disease, but suggested that it may help the brain to cope with damage for longer, an idea known as cognitive reserve.

E. In the last fifteen years, however, the picture has become more complicated. Several large studies, some involving thousands of participants, found no clear difference between bilinguals and monolinguals on tests of attention and task-switching. Critics also argued that studies finding an advantage were more likely to be published than those that did not. The debate continues, and many researchers now believe that if a general cognitive advantage exists, it is smaller and less consistent than was once claimed.

F. What is not in doubt is that bilingualism brings practical, social and cultural benefits. Speaking two languages allows people to communicate with a wider range of people, to keep close links with family and community, and to enjoy literature and media in more than one language. For these reasons, many educators argue that the case for supporting children’s home languages does not depend on proving that bilingualism makes them better at mental tests.

paragraphs: A. Maps are among the oldest forms of human communication. A clay tablet found in Iraq, made around 600 BC, shows the world as a flat disc surrounded by a ring of water, with the city of Babylon near its centre. Such early maps were not intended to be accurate guides for travellers. They expressed how people understood their place in the world, mixing geography with religion and myth.

B. The ancient Greeks took a more scientific approach. In the third century BC, the scholar Eratosthenes, working in Alexandria, estimated the circumference of the Earth by comparing the angle of the sun’s rays in two cities at the same time of year. His result was remarkably close to the true figure. Later, the astronomer Ptolemy described how to represent the curved surface of the Earth on a flat surface and listed the positions of thousands of places using a system similar to latitude and longitude.

C. During the medieval period, much of this knowledge was preserved and developed by scholars in the Islamic world. In 1154, the geographer al-Idrisi completed a large map of the known world for King Roger II of Sicily, based on the reports of travellers and merchants. It was considered the most accurate world map of its time, and, unlike most European maps today, it placed south at the top.

D. The age of European ocean exploration created a demand for maps that sailors could use to plot a course. In 1569, the Flemish mapmaker Gerardus Mercator published a world map on which lines of constant compass direction appeared as straight lines. This made it extremely useful for navigation. However, the projection greatly enlarges areas far from the equator, so that Greenland appears almost as large as Africa, although Africa is in fact about fourteen times bigger.

E. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, governments began to survey their territories systematically. Using a method called triangulation, surveyors measured angles between distant points with great precision and calculated distances mathematically. The work was slow: the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, which began in 1802, took several decades. One of its achievements was the first accurate measurement of the height of the world’s highest mountain.

F. Today, most maps are produced digitally from aerial photographs and satellite images, and global positioning systems allow anyone with a phone to see their exact location. Yet the basic problem that Ptolemy described has not disappeared: every flat map of a round Earth involves some distortion. Mapmakers still have to choose which features — shape, area, distance or direction — to represent faithfully and which to sacrifice.

A. Along tropical and subtropical coastlines, where the land meets the sea, grow forests unlike any others. Mangroves are trees and shrubs that can survive in salty water and in mud that contains very little oxygen. They are found in more than one hundred countries, and although they cover only a small fraction of the world’s forested area, they provide a wide range of benefits to both nature and people.

B. Mangroves have developed several ways of coping with their difficult environment. Many species have roots that grow above the ground, either arching out from the trunk or rising vertically from the mud like pencils. These aerial roots take in oxygen from the air. To deal with salt, some species prevent most of it from entering their roots, while others take it in and then release it through special glands on their leaves, where it can sometimes be seen as small white crystals.

C. The tangled roots of mangroves provide shelter for young fish, crabs and shrimps, protecting them from larger predators. Scientists estimate that a large proportion of the fish caught in some tropical regions spend part of their lives in mangrove forests. The forests also support birds, reptiles and mammals, and in parts of Asia they are home to animals such as the fishing cat and, in the Sundarbans of India and Bangladesh, the Bengal tiger.

D. Mangroves also protect people. Their dense roots reduce the energy of waves and help to protect coastal communities from storms. After the Indian Ocean tsunami of 2004, some studies reported that villages behind healthy mangrove forests suffered less damage than those where the forests had been cleared, although other factors, such as the shape of the coastline, also played a part. In addition, the roots trap sediment, which helps the land to build up and can slow erosion.

E. A further benefit has attracted attention in recent years. Mangrove forests store large amounts of carbon, not only in their trees but especially in the waterlogged soil beneath them, where dead plant material decays very slowly. Per hectare, they can store several times as much carbon as many forests on land. When mangroves are destroyed, much of this carbon may be released into the atmosphere.

F. Despite their value, mangroves have been cleared on a large scale, particularly to make way for shrimp farms, rice fields and coastal development. Since 1980, a significant share of the world’s mangroves has been lost, although the rate of loss has slowed in recent years. Restoration projects have had mixed results: planting large numbers of seedlings in the wrong places has often failed, and experts now emphasise restoring the natural flow of water so that mangroves can return by themselves.

A. Every wave of new technology has been accompanied by fears that machines would take away people’s jobs. In early nineteenth-century England, groups of textile workers known as Luddites broke into factories and destroyed weaving machines that threatened their livelihoods. In the 1960s, government committees in the United States studied the possibility that automation would lead to mass unemployment. In both cases, the worst fears were not realised: total employment continued to grow, although many individual workers suffered.

B. Economists explain this pattern in several ways. Machines that make goods cheaper leave people with more money to spend on other things, which creates jobs elsewhere in the economy. New technologies also create entirely new kinds of work. Few people in 1980 could have imagined that millions would one day be employed in developing websites or managing social media. Finally, machines often take over particular tasks rather than whole jobs, changing what workers do rather than replacing them completely.

C. The automatic teller machine, or ATM, is often cited as an example. When ATMs spread in the United States from the 1970s onwards, many people expected the number of bank tellers to fall sharply. Instead, it rose for several decades. Because ATMs reduced the cost of running a branch, banks opened more branches, and tellers spent less time handling cash and more time advising customers and selling services.

D. Some researchers argue that recent developments may be different. Earlier machines mainly replaced physical work and routine tasks that followed clear rules. Advances in artificial intelligence allow computers to perform tasks that once seemed to require human judgement, such as recognising images, translating text and analysing documents. A widely discussed study published in 2013 estimated that almost half of jobs in the United States were at high risk of automation within two decades, although later studies using different methods produced much lower figures.

E. Even where total employment does not fall, the effects of automation may be unequal. Research suggests that in recent decades, jobs requiring medium levels of skill, such as clerical and some factory work, have declined in many wealthy countries, while both highly paid professional jobs and lower-paid service jobs have grown. This process, sometimes called job polarisation, may contribute to rising inequality.

F. How societies should respond is a matter of debate. Many economists emphasise education and retraining, so that workers can move into new occupations as old ones disappear. Others argue for stronger social protection, such as unemployment insurance and support for workers who change careers later in life. A smaller group supports more radical ideas, such as a basic income paid to every citizen. What most agree on is that the outcome is not determined by technology alone, but by the choices that governments, businesses and workers make.

reading.passageTitle: Reading Passage 1: The Journey of Tea
paragraphs: A. Tea is the most widely consumed drink in the world after water. All true tea comes from a single plant, Camellia sinensis, an evergreen shrub that originated in the region where China, India and Myanmar meet. According to Chinese tradition, tea was discovered when leaves blew into a pot of boiling water, but historians believe that it was first used as a medicine, and only later became an everyday drink.

B. During the Tang dynasty, which lasted from the seventh to the tenth century, tea drinking spread throughout China. Around 760, the writer Lu Yu produced The Classic of Tea, the first known book devoted to the subject, describing how tea should be grown, prepared and served. At that time, tea leaves were usually steamed and pressed into hard cakes, which were broken up and boiled. Loose-leaf tea, steeped in hot water as most people drink it today, became common several centuries later.

C. Tea reached Japan with Buddhist monks, who used it to stay awake during long periods of meditation. Over time, the Japanese developed an elaborate ceremony in which powdered green tea is prepared and served according to precise rules. The ceremony was shaped in the sixteenth century by the tea master Sen no Rikyu, who emphasised simplicity, calm and respect between host and guest.

D. Tea arrived in Europe in the early seventeenth century, carried by Dutch traders. At first it was an expensive luxury, but it became fashionable in Britain after the marriage of King Charles II to the Portuguese princess Catherine of Braganza in 1662, who was already fond of the drink. By the eighteenth century, tea was so popular that high taxes led to widespread smuggling, and it was estimated that more tea entered Britain illegally than legally.

E. For a long time, China was the only major source of tea, and Britain paid for it largely with silver. To reduce this dependence, the British East India Company sought to grow tea in its own territories. In the 1830s, tea plants were discovered growing wild in Assam, in north-east India, and plantations were soon established there and later in Ceylon, now Sri Lanka. The botanist Robert Fortune also smuggled plants and seeds out of China in the 1840s, together with knowledge of how they were processed.

F. The different types of tea — white, green, oolong and black — all come from the same plant. What distinguishes them is mainly how the leaves are processed after picking, and in particular how much they are allowed to oxidise. Green tea is heated soon after picking to stop oxidation, which keeps the leaves green, while black tea is fully oxidised, giving it a darker colour and stronger flavour. Oolong lies between the two.

A. Octopuses have long fascinated scientists because they combine a soft, boneless body with behaviour that appears remarkably intelligent. An octopus has around five hundred million neurons, a number comparable to that of a dog, but the way these nerve cells are arranged is very different from that of vertebrates. About two-thirds of them are located not in the brain but in the arms, which can respond to touch and taste with a considerable degree of independence.

B. Laboratory studies have shown that octopuses can solve a variety of problems. They can learn to open jars to reach food inside, find their way through simple mazes, and distinguish between objects of different shapes and brightness. In some experiments, octopuses appeared to learn by watching other octopuses perform a task, although later attempts to repeat these results were not always successful.

C. In the wild, octopuses show a striking ability to use objects. Researchers in Indonesia filmed veined octopuses carrying coconut shells across the sea floor and assembling them into shelters when needed. Because the animals carried the shells for later use, rather than simply hiding in them when they found them, some scientists consider this one of the first known examples of tool use by an invertebrate.

D. Perhaps the most dramatic feature of octopuses is their ability to change colour and texture within a fraction of a second. Their skin contains thousands of cells filled with pigment, called chromatophores, which can be expanded or contracted by muscles controlled by the nervous system. Some species can also raise small bumps on their skin to imitate rocks or seaweed. Curiously, most octopuses are thought to be colour-blind, and researchers are still investigating how they match their surroundings so precisely.

E. Keepers of octopuses in aquariums report that individual animals behave differently, with some appearing curious and bold and others shy. There are stories of octopuses escaping from their tanks at night, squirting water at particular members of staff and turning off lights by directing jets of water at them. Such accounts are difficult to test scientifically, but they have encouraged researchers to study personality in these animals.

F. Despite their abilities, most octopuses live for only one or two years. Females usually die shortly after their eggs hatch, having stopped eating while guarding them. This short life raises a puzzle for scientists, because intelligence is usually associated with long-lived social animals that learn from others over many years. In octopuses, it seems to have evolved in solitary animals with brief lives, perhaps because hunting and avoiding predators in a complex environment required flexible behaviour.

A. In 1906, the British scientist Francis Galton visited a country fair where people were invited to guess the weight of an ox once it had been slaughtered and prepared. Galton collected around eight hundred guesses and calculated their middle value. To his surprise, the result was within one per cent of the true weight, closer than most individual guesses, including those of people who claimed expert knowledge. The idea that a group can be wiser than its members has since been called the wisdom of crowds.

B. Research suggests that crowds are wise only under certain conditions. The most important is independence: each person must form a judgement without being influenced by the others. When individual errors are independent, they tend to cancel each other out, so that the average is accurate. Diversity also matters, because people who approach a problem in different ways are less likely to make the same mistakes.

C. When these conditions are not met, groups can perform badly. If people can see others’ answers before giving their own, they tend to copy them, and the diversity of opinion that makes crowds accurate is lost. In one experiment, participants answered factual questions either alone or after being told the answers of others. Social information made the answers more similar to each other, but not more accurate, and it made participants more confident.

D. The principle has many practical applications. Prediction markets, in which people buy and sell shares whose value depends on whether a future event happens, have produced forecasts of elections and other events that compare well with expert predictions. Online review systems and some forecasting tournaments also rely on combining many independent judgements. Even within a single person, averaging two separate estimates made at different times can produce a more accurate answer than either estimate alone.

E. Crowds are not always reliable, however. Financial bubbles, in which prices rise far above any reasonable value before collapsing, show how a crowd can be carried away when people follow each other rather than thinking independently. In meetings, the views of the first or most senior speaker may dominate the discussion. Some organisations therefore ask members to write down their opinions privately before any discussion begins.

F. The wisdom of crowds does not mean that expertise is useless. For many technical questions, the judgement of a few well-informed people is more reliable than the average of many uninformed ones. Researchers increasingly suggest combining the two: asking a diverse group of knowledgeable people for independent estimates and then averaging them. The lesson of Galton’s ox, they argue, is not that anyone’s guess is as good as anyone else’s, but that the way judgements are collected matters a great deal.

paragraphs: A. In the 1960s, the Aral Sea, which lies between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, was the fourth-largest lake in the world, covering about 68,000 square kilometres. It supported a fishing industry that employed tens of thousands of people, and the port towns of Aralsk in the north and Moynaq in the south were busy centres of fish processing. The sea was fed by two great rivers, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, which carry water from the mountains of Central Asia.

B. From the 1960s, the Soviet government greatly expanded irrigated agriculture in the region, especially for growing cotton. Large amounts of water were taken from the two rivers through a network of canals, many of which were unlined, so that much of the water soaked into the ground or evaporated before it reached the fields. As a result, the volume of water reaching the Aral Sea fell sharply, and the sea began to shrink.

C. The consequences were severe. By the 1980s, the shoreline had retreated many kilometres from the old ports, leaving fishing boats stranded in the desert. As the water evaporated, the remaining sea became much saltier, and most native fish species disappeared. The commercial fishing industry collapsed, and many people left the region in search of work.

D. The exposed seabed created further problems. It was covered with salt and with residues of fertilisers and pesticides that had been washed into the sea from farmland. Strong winds carried this dust over large areas, affecting farmland and, according to many reports, the health of local people. The climate around the sea also changed: without the moderating effect of a large body of water, summers became hotter and winters colder.

E. By the late 1980s, the sea had split into two separate bodies of water: the smaller North Aral Sea and the larger South Aral Sea. In 2005, with support from the World Bank, Kazakhstan completed the Kokaral Dam, which prevents water from the Syr Darya flowing into the southern part. The level of the North Aral Sea rose by several metres within a few years, the water became less salty, and fish returned, allowing a fishing industry to restart.

F. The South Aral Sea has had a different fate. Its eastern basin dried up almost completely in 2014, and the remaining water is extremely salty. In Uzbekistan, efforts have focused on planting drought-resistant shrubs, such as saxaul, on the former seabed to hold the soil in place and reduce dust storms. Most experts believe that restoring the entire sea is no longer possible, but the recovery of the northern part shows that careful water management can bring real improvements.

A. More than three hundred million tonnes of plastic are produced every year, and only a small proportion is recycled. Much of the rest is buried in landfill, burned or released into the environment, where it can remain for centuries. Scientists have therefore been interested in a surprising possibility: that living organisms could help to break plastic down.

B. In 2016, a team of Japanese researchers reported that they had found a bacterium capable of feeding on PET, the plastic used to make most drinks bottles. They discovered it in samples collected outside a bottle-recycling plant, where it had apparently adapted to the plastic waste around it. The bacterium, later named Ideonella sakaiensis, produces two enzymes that work together to break PET into its basic chemical building blocks, which it then uses as food.

C. The natural process is very slow: in the original experiments, it took the bacterium about six weeks to break down a thin film of plastic at a comfortable temperature. Scientists have since tried to improve the enzymes. In 2018, researchers studying the structure of one enzyme accidentally produced a version that worked faster than the original. Later work, using computer models and laboratory testing, created enzymes able to break down PET in a matter of hours or days.

D. One attraction of this approach is that the building blocks produced by the enzymes can be used to make new plastic of the same quality as the original. Conventional mechanical recycling, in which plastic is cleaned, melted and remoulded, tends to reduce its quality each time, so that bottles are often turned into lower-value products such as clothing fibres. Enzymatic recycling could, in principle, allow the same material to be used again and again.

E. Several companies are now developing enzymatic recycling on an industrial scale, and the first factories have been planned. However, important obstacles remain. Many enzymes work best at temperatures close to the point at which PET begins to soften, and plastic waste must usually be ground into small pieces before treatment. The cost of the process must also be competitive with producing new plastic from oil, which is often very cheap.

F. Researchers stress that such technologies are not a solution to plastic pollution on their own. Enzymes that break down PET do not work on most other common plastics, such as polyethylene and polypropylene, and releasing plastic-eating organisms into the environment would raise serious questions about their effects. Reducing the amount of plastic produced and improving collection, they argue, remain the most important steps.

A. Almost everyone has had the experience of hearing a song and suddenly remembering a particular period of their life. Psychologists have found that music is especially effective at triggering memories of events from the past, and that these memories are often vivid and emotional. Studies in which participants listened to popular songs from different decades found that songs from their late teens and early twenties were most strongly associated with personal memories.

B. One reason for the strength of these links may be the way music is processed in the brain. Listening to music involves many areas at once, including those concerned with hearing, movement, emotion and memory. Brain-imaging studies have found that familiar music activates a region near the front of the brain known as the medial prefrontal cortex, which is also involved in recalling information about ourselves. The more familiar and emotionally significant the music, the stronger the response.

C. These findings have attracted particular interest from people caring for patients with dementia. Even when patients have lost the ability to remember recent events or to recognise members of their family, many can still sing the words of songs they learned when they were young. Researchers believe that musical memory may be stored partly in areas of the brain that are damaged relatively late in the course of the disease.

D. Music-based activities have therefore been introduced in many care homes. Some programmes create personal playlists of songs that were important to each resident. Care staff report that listening to these songs can calm patients who are anxious, encourage them to talk and help them to connect with their families. A number of small studies have found reductions in agitation and in the use of some medicines, although larger trials have produced more mixed results.

E. Music has also been studied as a tool for learning. Many people learned the alphabet as children by singing it, and some research suggests that setting information to a melody can help people remember it. However, the benefits appear to be limited. Music helps most when the melody is simple and familiar, and when the information is short; for longer and more complex material, learning the tune itself may take too much effort.

F. Not all findings about music and the mind have stood up to closer examination. In 1993, a study reported that students who listened to a piece by Mozart performed better on a spatial reasoning task for a short time afterwards. The result was widely reported as evidence that listening to classical music makes people more intelligent, an idea that became known as the Mozart effect. Later studies found that the effect was small, short-lived and probably caused by improved mood and alertness rather than anything special about Mozart’s music.

paragraphs: A. Silk is produced by the caterpillar of a moth, Bombyx mori, which spins a cocoon of a single continuous thread before it changes into an adult. According to Chinese legend, the discovery was made by an empress who noticed a cocoon fall into her cup of hot tea and unwind into a fine thread. Whatever the truth of the story, archaeological evidence shows that silk was being produced in China at least five thousand years ago.

B. Producing silk is a demanding process. The caterpillars, usually called silkworms, eat only the leaves of the mulberry tree, and large quantities are needed: in its life of about a month, a single silkworm multiplies its weight roughly ten thousand times. When the cocoons are complete, most are heated to prevent the moths from emerging and breaking the thread. The cocoons are then softened in hot water, and the ends of several threads are found and wound together onto a reel.

C. For many centuries, China guarded the secret of silk production carefully. Silk cloth was exported along the trade routes that later became known as the Silk Road, and in Rome it was so highly valued that some writers complained about the amount of gold leaving the empire to pay for it. According to a story told by the historian Procopius, silkworm eggs were finally smuggled to the Byzantine Empire in the sixth century by monks who hid them inside hollow walking sticks.

D. Silk production gradually spread across Asia and Europe. Central Asian cities became important centres of weaving, and in the Fergana Valley, which includes parts of modern Uzbekistan, silk has been produced for many centuries. The town of Margilan is still famous for atlas and adras, traditional fabrics decorated with patterns created by a technique known as ikat, in which the threads are tied and dyed before weaving so that the design appears as the cloth is woven.

E. In Europe, Italy and France developed major silk industries from the late medieval period onwards, and in the nineteenth century the French city of Lyon was one of the world’s leading producers of silk cloth. In the 1850s and 1860s, however, a disease spread among silkworms in Europe, causing heavy losses. The scientist Louis Pasteur was asked to investigate, and he showed how infected eggs could be identified and removed, helping the industry to recover.

F. In the twentieth century, synthetic fibres such as nylon, introduced in the 1930s, replaced silk in many uses, including stockings and parachutes. Nevertheless, silk remains valued for its softness, strength and shine, and China and India are now the world’s largest producers. Scientists are also exploring new uses for silk proteins, from surgical stitches to coatings that help fresh fruit last longer.

A. In 1995, after an absence of about seventy years, wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park in the United States. Wolves had been deliberately eliminated from the park in the early twentieth century, when they were regarded as dangerous predators that threatened livestock and game animals. Their return, with animals brought from Canada, was one of the most closely studied wildlife experiments in history.

B. Without wolves, the number of elk in Yellowstone had grown considerably. The elk grazed heavily on young trees and shrubs, particularly willow and aspen along the rivers. When wolves returned, they began to hunt elk, and the elk population fell. According to some researchers, the elk also changed their behaviour, spending less time in open river valleys where they were more likely to be attacked.

C. Some scientists argued that these changes set off a chain of effects through the ecosystem, a process known as a trophic cascade. With less grazing, willows and aspens were able to grow again in some places. Beavers, which use willow for food and building, increased in number, and their dams created ponds that provided habitats for fish, birds and amphibians. The return of vegetation along the riverbanks was even said to have reduced erosion.

D. This account became widely known and was presented in popular films as evidence that a single species can transform a whole landscape. However, some ecologists have questioned how strong the effects really were. They point out that the recovery of trees has been patchy, and that other factors were changing at the same time. Hunting by humans outside the park, a series of dry years, and the growing number of bears and cougars, which also prey on young elk, all affected elk numbers.

E. The question of whether elk really avoided risky areas has also been debated. Studies using GPS collars found that elk did not always move away from places where wolves were common, and that their behaviour depended on the time of day and the season. Some researchers concluded that the so-called landscape of fear was weaker than had been suggested, while others continued to find evidence of it in particular areas.

F. Most scientists agree that the reintroduction of wolves has had important effects, but they emphasise that ecosystems are complex and that it is rarely possible to attribute changes to a single cause. The Yellowstone experience has nevertheless influenced debates about bringing back large predators elsewhere, including the return of wolves to parts of Europe. In such cases, the interests of farmers, whose animals may be attacked, must be balanced against the goals of conservation.

A. Few children today have many opportunities to be bored. Smartphones, tablets and organised activities fill much of their free time, and many parents feel that it is their responsibility to keep their children entertained. Yet a growing number of psychologists and educators argue that occasional boredom may be valuable, because it encourages children to use their imagination and to find their own ways of occupying themselves.

B. Boredom is usually defined as an unpleasant state in which a person wants to be engaged in a satisfying activity but is unable to find one. Researchers distinguish it from relaxation, which is pleasant and chosen. Because boredom is uncomfortable, it acts as a signal: it tells us that what we are doing is not rewarding and pushes us to look for something more meaningful. In this sense, it has been compared with hunger or pain.

C. Several studies have explored the link between boredom and creativity. In one well-known experiment, carried out in Britain, participants were first asked to copy numbers from a telephone directory for fifteen minutes, a deliberately dull task. They were then asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. Those who had done the boring task came up with more ideas than a group that had not, and the effect was stronger when the first task was even more boring.

D. The explanation proposed by the researchers is that boredom leads the mind to wander, and daydreaming can produce unexpected connections between ideas. However, they also note that not all forms of boredom are helpful. Chronic boredom, which lasts for long periods, has been linked with anxiety, overeating and risky behaviour, especially among teenagers who feel they have nothing meaningful to do.

E. Critics of the boredom-creativity research point out that the experiments were mostly small and carried out with adults rather than children. The tasks used to measure creativity, such as listing uses for everyday objects, may not reflect the kind of creativity that matters in real life. Some later studies have also failed to find a clear effect. More research is needed, they argue, before firm advice can be given to parents.

F. Nevertheless, many educators suggest that children benefit from unstructured time in which no activity is planned for them. They do not recommend leaving children with nothing to do for long periods, but rather allowing them to experience short spells of boredom and to find their own solutions. Simple materials, such as paper, cardboard boxes or a garden, can provide the starting point for games and projects that children invent for themselves.

Learning a language online used to mean watching recorded lessons alone at a computer. Today, many learners prefer live classes with a real teacher, even if the teacher is in another country. Some say the most important advantage is flexibility: lessons can be taken early in the morning or late at night, around work and family duties.

However, online learning is not suitable for everyone. Learners who find it difficult to organise their time often stop after a few weeks, especially when nobody checks whether they have done their homework. Teachers report that students who set a fixed time for lessons every week are far more likely to continue.

Another concern is speaking practice. In a large online group, each learner may speak for only a few minutes. For this reason, some schools now limit online groups to six students, while others offer extra conversation sessions with a partner. Many learners also use apps between lessons, although most teachers see these as a supplement rather than a replacement for real conversation.

A. For centuries, the Silk Road connected China with the Mediterranean, and cities such as Samarkand and Bukhara grew rich from the trade that passed through them. Merchants stopped in these cities to rest, exchange goods and find fresh animals for the next stage of the journey.

B. The routes carried far more than silk. Paper, spices, glass, metals and horses moved in both directions. Just as important were ideas: religions, scientific knowledge and artistic styles spread along the same roads as the goods.

C. Travel was slow and often dangerous. Caravans could take months to cross deserts and mountains, and they faced extreme heat, cold and the risk of attack. Caravanserais — inns built at regular distances along the routes — offered shelter and safety for travellers and their animals.

D. In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, the importance of the land routes declined. European traders increasingly used sea routes, which could carry larger loads more cheaply, and political changes made some parts of the land routes less secure.

E. Today, interest in the Silk Road has returned. Historic buildings in Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva attract visitors from all over the world, and many caravanserais have been restored. Tourism has become an important source of income for the region.

F. At the same time, new transport projects — railways, roads and pipelines — are once again linking Central Asia with China and Europe. Some writers describe these as a “new Silk Road”, although the goods they carry are very different from those of the past.

Many people believe that creativity is a rare talent that some people are born with and others are not. Psychologists, however, increasingly see it as a skill that can be developed with practice. Studies of successful artists and scientists show that they often produce a large number of ideas, most of which are never used. Quantity, it seems, is one of the routes to quality.

One factor that appears to help is a period of rest after hard work on a problem. People frequently report that a solution came to them while they were walking or taking a shower, rather than while they were sitting at a desk. Researchers believe that during such breaks the mind continues to work on the problem without our being aware of it.

Fear of criticism, on the other hand, seems to reduce creativity. When people expect their ideas to be judged harshly, they tend to suggest only safe and familiar solutions. For this reason, many organisations separate the stage of producing ideas from the stage of evaluating them.

Finally, creativity often grows from combining knowledge from different fields. An engineer who studies biology, or a designer who learns about psychology, may notice connections that specialists miss. This suggests that schools which encourage students to explore several subjects may be preparing them better for creative work.

The idea that the language we speak shapes the way we think has fascinated scholars for more than a century. In its strongest form, the claim is that speakers of different languages live in different mental worlds, unable to understand concepts for which their language has no words. Few researchers today accept this extreme position, not least because translation between languages, though imperfect, is clearly possible.

A weaker version of the idea, however, has received considerable support. Experiments suggest that language can influence what people notice and remember. For example, languages differ in how they describe the position of objects. Some rely on terms such as “left” and “right”, which depend on the speaker’s body, while others use fixed directions such as north and south. Speakers of the second type of language tend to remember the arrangement of objects in terms of those fixed directions, even in tasks that do not involve speaking.

Critics point out that such differences may be caused not by language itself but by the culture and environment in which the language is used. A community that lives in open landscape may need fixed directions for practical reasons, and the language simply reflects this need. Separating the effect of language from the effect of culture is therefore one of the central difficulties in this area of research.

Whatever the final answer, the debate has had practical consequences. It has encouraged researchers to study a wider range of languages, many of which are spoken by small communities and are at risk of disappearing. Each of these languages, linguists argue, represents a unique way of organising human experience, and its loss would be a loss to science as well as to its speakers.

In many cities, more and more people are choosing to cycle to work. For some, the main reason is money: a bicycle costs far less to run than a car, and there are no parking charges. Others say they cycle because it allows them to exercise without having to find extra time for the gym.

City councils have responded in different ways. Some have built separate cycle lanes, so that cyclists do not have to share the road with buses and lorries. Where such lanes exist, the number of cyclists usually rises quickly. Other cities have introduced bike-sharing schemes, which let people rent a bicycle for a short journey using a mobile phone.

Not everyone is enthusiastic, though. Some drivers complain that cycle lanes make the roads narrower and traffic slower. Cyclists, for their part, often say that the biggest problem is not traffic but the weather: in winter, many of them leave their bicycles at home and take public transport instead.

A. In towns and villages across Central Asia, the choyxona, or tea house, has long been more than a place to drink tea. Traditionally, men gathered there in the late afternoon to talk about the day’s news, discuss family matters and settle small disagreements.

B. A typical tea house was built near water — a canal, a stream or a pool — and shaded by large trees. Guests sat on wide wooden platforms covered with carpets and cushions, and in summer the cool air from the water made these places especially popular.

C. Green tea was the usual drink, served in small bowls rather than cups. The host poured a little tea into a bowl and returned it to the pot several times before serving, a custom that is said to help the tea develop its full flavour.

D. Food also played an important part. On special occasions, a large dish of plov was cooked in a huge pot over an open fire, and preparing it was often the job of an experienced cook who was respected throughout the neighbourhood.

E. During the twentieth century, as cities grew and lifestyles changed, many traditional tea houses disappeared. Younger people increasingly preferred cafés and restaurants, and the custom of meeting every afternoon became less common.

F. Recently, however, the tea house has enjoyed something of a revival. Modern versions combine traditional decoration with comfortable furniture and Wi-Fi, and they attract families and tourists as well as the older men who were once their main visitors.

Teenagers are often described as lazy because they find it hard to get up in the morning. Scientists, however, have discovered that their behaviour has a biological cause. During adolescence, the body begins to produce the sleep hormone melatonin later in the evening, so most teenagers do not feel tired until around eleven o’clock at night.

Because school usually starts early, many teenagers do not get the eight to ten hours of sleep that doctors recommend. A lack of sleep can affect concentration, memory and mood, and it has been linked to lower marks in subjects such as mathematics.

Some schools have experimented with a later start to the school day. In several studies, students who began lessons an hour later slept longer, were absent less often and reported feeling less stressed. Teachers also noticed that pupils were more alert in morning lessons.

Changing the timetable is not always easy, however. Parents may need to change their working hours, and bus companies must adjust their routes. Experts therefore suggest that families can also help by limiting the use of screens in the evening, because the light from phones can delay sleep even further.

It has become common to hear that the internet is changing the way we remember. Why, the argument goes, should anyone memorise a date, a phone number or a fact when it can be found in seconds? Some researchers have described a tendency to forget information that we expect to be able to look up later, and they have suggested that we now treat the internet as a kind of external memory.

This is not entirely new. Long before computers, people relied on books, diaries and other people to store information for them. Within families, for example, one person might be responsible for remembering birthdays while another keeps track of money. What has changed is the size and speed of the external store, and the fact that it is available almost everywhere.

Whether this is a problem depends partly on what we use our memory for. Critics argue that understanding a subject deeply requires knowledge stored in our own heads, because we can only connect ideas that we actually know. A person who must search for every basic fact, they say, will find it hard to think creatively or to notice when information is false.

Others are more optimistic. They point out that freeing the mind from routine facts may leave more capacity for analysis and judgement. The challenge for schools, in their view, is not to ban search engines but to teach students which knowledge is worth learning by heart and how to evaluate what they find online.

Volunteering means giving your time to help others without being paid. People volunteer in many ways: some help in hospitals or schools, some clean parks and rivers, and others support older people who live alone. In recent years, the number of young volunteers has grown in many countries.

Volunteers often say that they get as much from the experience as the people they help. They meet new friends, learn practical skills and feel more connected to their community. For students, volunteering can also be useful when applying for a job, because employers value experience of teamwork and responsibility.

However, organisations that use volunteers face some difficulties. Many people are keen at the start but stop coming after a few weeks. To keep volunteers, successful organisations give them clear tasks, thank them regularly and offer short training sessions. Some also let volunteers choose the hours that suit them best.

A. Bees are among the most important insects on Earth. By carrying pollen from one flower to another, they help plants to produce fruit and seeds. A large part of the food we eat, from apples to almonds, depends at least partly on this work.

B. Honeybees live in highly organised colonies. Each colony has a single queen, which lays the eggs, and thousands of female workers, which collect food, build the wax cells and look after the young. Male bees have only one role: to mate with a queen.

C. When a worker bee finds a good source of food, she returns to the hive and performs a “dance”. The direction and length of the dance tell other bees where the flowers are and how far away they are.

D. In many parts of the world, the number of bees has fallen sharply. Scientists believe there are several causes, including the loss of wild flowers, the use of certain chemicals on farms, diseases and changes in the climate.

E. Farmers and governments have started to respond. Some farmers now leave strips of wild flowers at the edges of their fields, and several countries have limited the use of chemicals that are particularly harmful to bees.

F. Ordinary people can help too. Planting flowers in gardens and on balconies, avoiding garden chemicals and buying honey from local beekeepers are all small steps that, taken together, can make a difference.

Fast fashion is the name given to clothes that are designed, produced and sold very quickly and at low prices. Instead of two collections a year, some shops now introduce new styles every week, encouraging customers to buy more often.

The low prices have a hidden cost. Producing clothes uses large amounts of water and energy, and many cheap garments are made from synthetic materials that are produced from oil. When these clothes are washed, tiny plastic fibres can enter rivers and the sea.

Another problem is waste. Because cheap clothes are often of poor quality, they wear out quickly, and many are thrown away after being worn only a few times. Most of these clothes end up in landfill, where they may take many years to break down.

Some consumers are changing their habits. Second-hand clothes shops and online platforms for swapping clothes have become more popular, especially among young people. Others are learning to repair their clothes instead of replacing them, and some brands now offer to take back old garments for recycling.

Does money make people happy? For most of the twentieth century, economists assumed that the answer was simply yes: the more people earned, the better off they were. When researchers began to ask people directly how satisfied they were with their lives, however, the picture turned out to be more complicated.

Surveys consistently show that, within a country, richer people report higher life satisfaction than poorer people. The effect is strongest at lower incomes, where extra money pays for basic needs such as food, housing and health care. At higher incomes, each additional amount of money seems to bring a smaller increase in satisfaction.

One explanation is that people judge their situation by comparing themselves with others. If everyone’s income rises at the same rate, nobody feels richer than their neighbours, and satisfaction may change very little. Another explanation is adaptation: people quickly get used to a higher standard of living, so that a new car or a bigger house soon stops giving pleasure.

Some researchers suggest that how people spend money matters as much as how much they have. Spending on experiences, such as travel or concerts, appears to produce longer-lasting satisfaction than spending on objects, and spending on other people — buying gifts or giving to charity — often makes the giver happier than spending on themselves.

Since 2020, millions of office workers around the world have started working from home for at least part of the week. For many, the biggest benefit is not having to travel. Time that was once spent in traffic or on crowded buses can now be used for sleep, exercise or family.

Working from home also has disadvantages. Some people find it hard to separate their work from their private life, and they end up answering emails late in the evening. Others miss the informal conversations with colleagues that often lead to new ideas and help new employees to learn.

As a result, many companies have chosen a “hybrid” model, in which staff spend some days in the office and some at home. Managers say that the office is now used mainly for meetings and teamwork, while tasks that need concentration are done at home. Some firms have reduced the size of their offices to save money.

A. Chess is one of the oldest board games still played today. Most historians believe that it developed in India around the sixth century, in a form known as chaturanga, and then spread to Persia, where it became known as shatranj.

B. From Persia, the game travelled west with traders and scholars. By the eleventh century it was known across the Arab world and in parts of Europe, and in the following centuries it became a favourite pastime of kings and nobles.

C. The game played at that time was slower than modern chess. The piece now called the queen could only move one square diagonally. In the late fifteenth century, players in southern Europe gave the queen much greater power, and the game became faster and more aggressive.

D. In the nineteenth century, chess became more organised. Clubs were founded in many cities, the first international tournaments were held, and players began to use clocks to limit the time each player could take.

E. The arrival of computers changed the game again. In 1997, a computer defeated the world champion in a match for the first time. Today, even a mobile phone can run a program that is stronger than any human player.

F. Rather than destroying interest in chess, computers have helped it grow. Players of all levels use programs to study and practise, and online platforms allow millions of people to play against opponents from other countries at any time of day.

In many cities, empty spaces between buildings are being turned into community gardens. On rooftops, in old car parks and even on the walls of buildings, residents are growing vegetables, fruit and flowers.

Supporters say that urban gardens bring several benefits. They provide fresh food for local people, and they make neighbourhoods greener and more attractive. Plants also help to cool the air in summer, which is important in cities where concrete and asphalt store heat.

Gardens can have social benefits as well. Working together on a shared project gives neighbours a reason to meet and talk, and many gardens organise events where children learn how food is grown. Doctors have also noted that gardening is good for mental health, as it reduces stress.

There are challenges, however. In some areas, the soil is polluted and must be replaced before anything can be planted. Water can be expensive, and gardens depend on volunteers who may lose interest. Some projects have also had to close when the land was sold for building.

False information is nothing new, but the speed at which it can now spread is. On social media, a misleading story can reach millions of people within hours, long before anyone has had time to check whether it is true. Studies of online sharing have found that false stories often travel further and faster than accurate ones, perhaps because they tend to be more surprising or emotional.

One common response has been fact-checking: journalists or independent organisations examine popular claims and publish corrections. Fact-checking can be effective, but it has limits. Corrections usually reach fewer people than the original story, and people who strongly believe a claim may reject a correction that challenges their views.

Some researchers have therefore turned to a different approach, sometimes called “prebunking”. Instead of correcting false stories after they appear, people are shown in advance the techniques that are often used to mislead, such as using emotional language, presenting false experts or offering only two options when there are more. The idea is similar to a vaccine: a weak exposure is meant to build resistance to the real thing.

Early results are encouraging, although it is not yet clear how long the effect lasts. Most experts agree that no single method will solve the problem. Platforms, schools, journalists and individual users all have a part to play, and perhaps the most valuable habit of all is simply to pause and check before sharing.

Street food is ready-to-eat food sold in public places such as markets, squares and the sides of busy roads. In many countries it is an important part of everyday life, because it is cheap, quick and often delicious. Millions of people buy their breakfast or lunch from street sellers every day.

For tourists, street food is often one of the highlights of a trip. It allows visitors to try local dishes and to see how ordinary people eat. Some cities now organise walking tours that take visitors from one food stall to another, with a guide who explains the history of each dish.

However, some people worry about hygiene. Sellers do not always have running water, and food may be kept outside in hot weather. For this reason, several cities have introduced rules that require street sellers to have a licence and to follow basic safety standards. Many sellers welcome these rules, because they help customers to trust them.

A. The Kyzylkum, whose name means “red sand”, is one of the largest deserts in Central Asia. It lies between two great rivers, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, and covers a large part of Uzbekistan as well as areas of Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan.

B. Life in the desert is shaped by extremes. Summers are very hot and dry, while winters can be surprisingly cold. Rain falls mainly in spring, and for a few weeks after it the desert is covered with grasses and flowers.

C. Although the land looks empty, it supports a variety of animals. Lizards, tortoises and snakes are common, and some larger animals, such as gazelles, are able to survive for long periods with very little water.

D. For centuries, people lived in the desert by moving with their animals in search of grass and water. Wells were extremely valuable, and their location was knowledge that families passed from one generation to the next.

E. In the twentieth century, the discovery of natural gas, gold and other minerals brought great changes. New towns were built for the workers, together with roads and railways that connected the desert to the rest of the country.

F. Today the desert also faces new pressures. Water taken from the rivers for farming has reduced the amount that reaches the region, and scientists are studying how changes in the climate may affect its plants and animals in the future.

Recycling is often presented as the simplest way for ordinary people to protect the environment. Yet in many countries only a small proportion of the plastic that is collected is actually turned into new products. The rest is burned, buried or sent abroad.

One reason is that there are many different types of plastic, and they cannot all be recycled together. Bottles, food containers and bags are often made from different materials, and if they are mixed, the quality of the recycled plastic falls.

Another problem is contamination. Containers that still have food or drink in them can spoil a whole load of material. For this reason, recycling centres ask people to rinse containers before putting them in the bin.

Many experts argue that recycling alone is not enough. They say that the most effective approach is to reduce the amount of plastic we use in the first place, for example by choosing products with less packaging, carrying reusable bags and bottles, and buying food loose rather than wrapped.

It is widely claimed that anyone can become an expert in almost any field if they practise for about ten thousand hours. The figure became famous through popular books, which drew on research into musicians and other high performers. The message was attractive because it suggested that success depends on effort rather than talent.

The researchers whose work inspired the claim have pointed out that it is a simplification. In their studies, the most important factor was not simply the number of hours but the type of practice. What they called “deliberate practice” involves working on specific weaknesses, usually with the guidance of a teacher, and receiving immediate feedback. Playing a piece of music that one already knows well does not count.

Later studies have also suggested that practice explains only part of the difference between people. In some activities, such as games and music, the amount of practice accounts for a considerable share of the variation in performance; in others, its role appears to be smaller. Factors such as the age at which people start, their working memory and even their personality may also matter.

None of this means that practice is unimportant. For most learners, a sensible conclusion is that how they practise matters at least as much as how long. Short, focused sessions that target particular problems, followed by honest feedback, are likely to be more valuable than many hours of comfortable repetition.

Board games, which many people thought had been replaced by video games, are enjoying a revival. In the last ten years, sales have increased in many countries, and special cafés where customers can play games while they eat and drink have opened in large cities.

One reason for their popularity is that board games bring people together face to face. Players say that, unlike most video games, board games make them talk, laugh and argue with friends and family around the same table. Some parents also like them because they give children a break from screens.

Modern board games are often very different from the classic games of the past. Many are cooperative, which means that players work together against the game rather than against each other. Others take several hours to play and have complex rules, so a member of staff in a games café may explain how to play.

A. Paper was invented in China more than two thousand years ago. Early paper was made from plant fibres, old cloth and fishing nets, which were soaked in water, beaten into a pulp and then spread on a screen to dry.

B. For several centuries, the method of making paper was known only in East Asia. According to a well-known story, the secret reached Samarkand in the eighth century, and the city soon became famous for producing paper of very high quality.

C. From Central Asia, papermaking spread to Baghdad, Damascus and Cairo, and later to Spain and Italy. Because paper was much cheaper than parchment made from animal skin, it allowed more books to be copied and more people to learn to read.

D. The invention of the printing press in Europe in the fifteenth century greatly increased the demand for paper. Mills powered by water were built along rivers, and paper became one of the most important materials of the modern world.

E. Until the nineteenth century, most paper in Europe was still made from old cloth, which was often in short supply. Inventors then found ways to make paper from wood, which made it far cheaper and allowed the production of newspapers for a mass audience.

F. Today, digital technology has reduced the use of paper in offices, but total demand remains high, partly because of the growth of online shopping and the cardboard boxes it requires. Recycling and responsibly managed forests have become important ways to limit the environmental impact.

Electric cars are becoming a common sight in many cities. Unlike traditional cars, they do not burn petrol or diesel, so they produce no exhaust gases while they are being driven. This can improve the air quality in busy streets.

However, electric cars are not completely clean. Making their batteries requires large amounts of energy and metals such as lithium, which must be mined. In addition, the electricity used to charge the cars may come from power stations that burn coal or gas.

For many drivers, the main concern is range — the distance a car can travel before its battery needs charging. Although modern cars can travel much further than early models, drivers still worry about finding a charging point on long journeys.

Governments in many countries are encouraging people to buy electric cars by offering lower taxes and free parking. As the number of charging points increases and battery prices fall, experts expect electric cars to become cheaper than petrol cars to buy as well as to run.

Most of us believe that we can do several things at once: answer a message while listening to a lecture, or follow a conversation while checking the news. Research on attention suggests that this belief is largely mistaken. Except for very simple or automatic activities, the brain does not truly perform two demanding tasks at the same time; instead, it switches rapidly between them.

Each switch has a cost. When we move our attention from one task to another, it takes time to remember where we were and what we were trying to do, and errors become more likely. These costs are small for a single switch but can add up to a considerable loss of time and accuracy over a working day.

Smartphones have made such switching more frequent. Notifications interrupt us many times an hour, and even when we ignore them, the expectation of a message can distract us. In one widely discussed study, students performed worse on tests of attention when their phones were simply on the desk, switched off, than when the phones were in another room — although later attempts to repeat this result have produced mixed findings.

What can be done? Researchers suggest that people who need to concentrate should group similar tasks together, turn off notifications for set periods and keep their phones out of sight. Some organisations have experimented with “quiet hours” during which meetings and messages are discouraged. The aim is not to reject technology but to use it in a way that protects our limited capacity for attention.

Keeping pets has become more popular in many cities in recent years. Cats and dogs are the most common, but some people prefer birds, fish or even reptiles. For many owners, a pet is not just an animal but a member of the family.

Research suggests that pets can be good for our health. Dog owners, for example, tend to walk more than people without dogs, and spending time with animals may lower stress. Pets can also be good company for people who live alone, especially older people.

However, owning a pet is a serious responsibility. Animals need food, exercise and visits to the vet, which can be expensive. A. The Olympic Games began in ancient Greece more than two and a half thousand years ago. They were held every four years at Olympia in honour of the god Zeus, and athletes came from many Greek cities to compete.

B. The ancient Games included running, wrestling, boxing, horse and chariot races, and the pentathlon, which combined five different events. Winners did not receive gold medals; instead, they were given a crown made of olive leaves, although they were often richly rewarded when they returned home.

C. The Games continued for more than a thousand years but finally came to an end in the late fourth century, when the Roman Empire, which by then ruled Greece, stopped supporting such traditional festivals.

D. The modern Olympic Games were the idea of a French educator, Pierre de Coubertin, who believed that sport could encourage peace and understanding between nations. The first modern Games were held in Athens in 1896.

E. Since then, the Games have grown enormously. Today thousands of athletes from more than two hundred countries take part, Winter Games have been added, and the Paralympic Games give athletes with disabilities the chance to compete at the highest level.

Around a third of all the food produced in the world is lost or wasted. Some is lost on farms and during transport, but in richer countries a large share is thrown away by shops, restaurants and households.

At home, food is often wasted because people buy more than they need. Special offers encourage shoppers to buy large quantities, and food is then forgotten at the back of the fridge until it goes bad. Confusion about date labels also plays a part: many people throw away food that is still safe to eat.

Wasting food is not only a waste of money. When food rots in landfill, it produces methane, a gas that contributes to climate change. In addition, all the water, land and energy used to grow and transport the food are wasted too.

There are simple ways to reduce waste. Planning meals for the week, making a shopping list and storing food correctly can all help. Some supermarkets now sell “ugly” fruit and vegetables at lower prices, and apps allow restaurants to sell leftover food cheaply at the end of the day.

For much of history, nostalgia — a longing for the past — was regarded as a kind of illness. In the seventeenth century, a Swiss doctor described it as a condition affecting soldiers who were far from home, and for a long time afterwards it was associated with sadness and an inability to cope with the present.

In recent decades, however, psychologists have begun to see nostalgia in a more positive light. Studies in which people are asked to recall a meaningful event from their past suggest that nostalgic memories often increase feelings of social connection and give life a sense of meaning. Interestingly, people tend to become more nostalgic when they feel lonely or anxious, which suggests that nostalgia may help them to restore their mood.

This does not mean that nostalgia is always helpful. When people constantly compare a disappointing present with an idealised past, nostalgia may make them less willing to accept change. Memories are also selective: we tend to remember the good parts of the past and forget the difficulties, so the “good old days” may never have been as good as we think.

Businesses are well aware of nostalgia’s power. Advertisers frequently use music, images and products from earlier decades to create a warm emotional response, and old brands are regularly brought back in their original packaging. For consumers, recognising this strategy may be the first step towards deciding whether they are buying a product or simply a feeling.

A gap year is a period, usually of several months to a year, that young people take between finishing school and starting university. During this time, some work to save money, while others travel, volunteer or learn new skills.

Supporters of gap years say that they help young people to become more independent and confident. Living away from home and dealing with new situations can teach them how to manage money, solve problems and communicate with people from different backgrounds. Some students also say that a gap year helped them to decide what they really wanted to study.

However, not everyone agrees that a gap year is a good idea. Some parents worry that their children will lose the habit of studying and find it difficult to return to education.
