A. The Ferghana Valley, surrounded by mountains, is one of the most fertile and densely populated regions of Central Asia. Rivers flowing down from the mountains bring water and rich soil, and for centuries farmers have grown fruit, grain and cotton there.

B. The valley is divided between three countries — Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan. The borders between them are long and complicated, and in some places villages belonging to one country are surrounded by the territory of another.

C. The towns of the valley are famous for their crafts. Margilan is known for its silk, Rishtan for its blue and green ceramics, and Kokand, once the capital of a powerful state, for its palaces and mosques.

D. Water has always been central to life in the valley. An ancient system of canals carries water from the rivers to the fields, and the right to use it was traditionally managed by local communities according to strict rules.

E. In the twentieth century, the area of land used for growing cotton was greatly increased. This brought income but also problems: large amounts of water were taken from the rivers, and in some areas the soil became salty and less productive.

F. In recent years, farmers have begun to grow a wider range of crops, including fruit and vegetables for export. At the same time, new roads and border crossings are making it easier for people and goods to move around the valley.

Noise is one of the most common forms of pollution in modern cities, yet it often receives less attention than polluted air or water. Traffic, aircraft, building work and loud music can all raise noise levels far above what is comfortable.

Long-term exposure to noise can harm health. It can disturb sleep, increase stress and, according to some studies, raise the risk of heart disease. Children who go to school near busy airports have been found to have more difficulty with reading.

Cities have tried various ways to reduce noise. Some have introduced lower speed limits at night, built walls along motorways and encouraged the use of quieter road surfaces. Electric buses, which are much quieter than diesel buses, are also helping in some places.

Trees and parks can help too, although their effect on noise levels is often smaller than people imagine. Perhaps their greatest value is that they offer residents quiet places where they can escape the noise for a while and recover from the stress of city life.

Public trust in science is often described as being in crisis. Commentators point to disputes over vaccines, climate change and nutrition as evidence that large numbers of people no longer believe what scientists tell them. Surveys, however, present a more nuanced picture: in many countries, scientists remain among the most trusted professional groups, considerably ahead of politicians and journalists.

Where distrust exists, it is often not a rejection of science as a whole but of particular findings that conflict with a person’s values, identity or interests. Someone may accept the science behind modern medicine while doubting research on climate change, especially if the policies associated with that research threaten their job or way of life.

Scientists themselves may sometimes contribute to the problem. When early results are presented with too much confidence and are later revised, members of the public may conclude that scientists cannot make up their minds. Yet changing conclusions in the light of new evidence is precisely how science is supposed to work; the difficulty lies in communicating uncertainty honestly without appearing unreliable.

Researchers who study science communication suggest several ways to build trust. Explaining not only what scientists know but how they know it, being open about uncertainty and listening to people’s concerns rather than simply correcting them all appear to help. Trust, they argue, is built slowly through relationships, and it cannot be demanded.

A. In the 1420s, Mirzo Ulugbek, the grandson of Amir Temur and ruler of Samarkand, built one of the greatest observatories of the medieval world. Ulugbek was not only a ruler but also a serious scientist, and he gathered around him some of the best mathematicians and astronomers of his time.

B. The most impressive part of the observatory was a huge instrument for measuring the position of the Sun, the Moon and the stars. Part of it was built into a deep trench cut into the hill, which helped to keep it stable and allowed very precise measurements.

C. The scientists working at the observatory produced a famous catalogue of stars, which gave the positions of around a thousand stars. For centuries it was among the most accurate works of its kind, and it was later translated and studied in Europe.

D. They also calculated the length of the year with remarkable accuracy. Their result differed from the value accepted today by only about a minute, an extraordinary achievement for observers working without telescopes.

E. After Ulugbek’s death in 1449, the observatory was no longer used, and over time it was destroyed. Its exact location was eventually forgotten, and for several centuries the achievements of the Samarkand astronomers were known mainly from manuscripts.

F. In 1908, an archaeologist discovered the remains of the observatory, including the underground part of the great instrument. Today the site is a museum, and it reminds visitors of a time when Samarkand was one of the world’s leading centres of science.

Many people feel more tired and less cheerful in winter, when the days are short. For most of them, this is a mild change in mood. For some, however, the effect is strong enough to affect their work and relationships, and doctors describe it as a form of depression linked to the seasons.

Light plays an important role in regulating our internal body clock. Exposure to bright light in the morning helps the body to know when to be awake and when to sleep. When days are short and people spend most of their time indoors, this signal becomes weaker.

One treatment that is often recommended is light therapy. Patients sit near a special lamp, which is much brighter than ordinary indoor lighting, for about half an hour each morning. Many people report that their mood improves within a few weeks.

There are also simple steps that anyone can take. Going outside during the brightest part of the day, even when it is cloudy, can help. Regular exercise and keeping a fixed time for going to bed and getting up are also recommended, as both support a healthy body clock.

Every day, each of us makes a large number of decisions, from what to eat for breakfast to how to respond to a difficult email. Some psychologists have proposed that the ability to make good decisions, or to resist temptation, depends on a limited mental resource that is gradually used up during the day. According to this idea, sometimes called “decision fatigue”, people who have made many choices become more likely to take the easy option or to avoid deciding at all.

The idea quickly became popular outside psychology. Business writers advised readers to make important decisions early in the day, and some well-known executives explained that they wore the same type of clothes every day in order to save their mental energy for more important matters.

In recent years, however, the theory has faced serious challenges. Several large studies that tried to repeat the original experiments failed to find the same effect, and some researchers have argued that the results may depend partly on what people believe about their own willpower. People who think that their self-control is unlimited, for instance, appear less likely to show signs of fatigue.

This does not mean that tiredness has no effect on decisions; long working hours, lack of sleep and hunger clearly influence how well we think. What remains uncertain is whether there is a single resource that every decision consumes. For practical purposes, the safest advice may simply be that important choices deserve time and attention, and should not be made when we are exhausted or rushed.

Public libraries were once mainly places where people borrowed books and studied in silence. Today, many libraries are changing. In addition to books, they lend e-books, films and even tools, and they offer free internet access to people who do not have it at home.

Many libraries also organise activities for different groups. Children can attend story sessions, teenagers can join coding clubs, and older people can take classes on how to use smartphones. Some libraries have special rooms where small businesses can hold meetings.

Not everyone welcomes these changes. Some regular users complain that libraries have become noisy and that there is less space for books. Librarians reply that they must attract new visitors in order to survive, and that most libraries still have quiet areas for reading and study.

A. Bridges have been built for thousands of years, from simple logs laid across streams to structures several kilometres long. Whatever their size, they all have the same basic purpose: to carry a load safely across an obstacle such as a river, a valley or a road.

B. Among the oldest types is the arch bridge. The curved shape of the arch carries the weight of the bridge outwards to the supports at each end. The Romans built many stone arch bridges, and some of them are still in use today, nearly two thousand years later.

C. The development of iron and later steel in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries allowed engineers to build much longer bridges. These materials are strong but relatively light, and they made it possible to cross wide rivers and deep valleys that had previously been impossible to bridge.

D. Suspension bridges, in which the road hangs from huge cables supported by tall towers, can cover the greatest distances. However, early examples showed that they could be dangerous in strong winds, and engineers had to learn how to make them more stable.

E. Modern engineers use computer models to test how a bridge will behave under different conditions, including heavy traffic, earthquakes and storms. Sensors fixed to the structure can also warn them if parts of a bridge begin to move or crack.

F. Bridges are not only practical structures; many have become symbols of the cities in which they stand. Some attract tourists from around the world, and their images appear on postcards, coins and banknotes.

Some companies have started to hold meetings while walking instead of sitting in a meeting room. Supporters say that walking meetings are a simple way to add physical activity to the working day, especially for people who spend many hours at a desk.

Walking may also help people to think. Several studies have found that people produce more creative ideas while walking than while sitting, and some participants say that conversations feel more relaxed and honest when people walk side by side rather than facing each other across a table.

Walking meetings are not suitable for every purpose, however. They work best for small groups of two or three people. It is difficult to look at documents or take detailed notes while walking, and noise from traffic can make it hard to hear.

Managers who use walking meetings suggest planning a route in advance, preferably through a park or a quiet street. They also advise telling participants beforehand so that they can wear comfortable shoes, and writing down the main decisions as soon as the meeting ends.

Machine translation has improved dramatically over the past decade. Systems based on large neural networks, trained on enormous collections of texts in many languages, now produce translations that are often fluent and, for many everyday purposes, perfectly adequate. For travellers, students and businesses, the ability to understand a text in an unfamiliar language within seconds has become almost taken for granted.

Yet fluency can be deceptive. Because modern systems are designed to produce natural-sounding sentences, their errors can be harder to spot than the obvious mistakes of earlier programs. A translation may read smoothly while changing the meaning of a sentence, omitting a negative or misunderstanding a technical term. In legal or medical contexts, such errors can have serious consequences.

Performance also varies greatly between languages. Systems work best for language pairs for which huge amounts of translated text are available, such as English and French. For languages with fewer digital resources, which include many languages spoken by millions of people, the quality is often considerably lower, although it is improving.

Professional translators have not disappeared, but their work is changing. Many now spend part of their time editing machine output rather than translating from scratch, and they increasingly focus on texts where cultural knowledge, style and accuracy matter most, such as literature, advertising and legal documents. For language learners, meanwhile, the question is no longer whether to use such tools, but how to use them without losing the benefits of working through a text themselves.

listening.context: Shahar bog‘lari haqida ma’ruza (B2 daraja, IELTS Part 4 uslubida).

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good afternoon. Today I want to talk about urban gardens — small areas of land in cities where residents grow their own fruit and vegetables.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Although they are often seen as a modern trend, community gardens have a long history. During periods of food shortage in the twentieth century, many governments actually encouraged people to grow food in parks and empty plots.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Today the motivation is rather different. In a recent survey of garden members in three European cities, the most common reason given was not saving money, but meeting neighbours. Food production came only third, after improving mental health.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Today I'd like to talk about urban beekeeping. Over the last decade, the number of hives in cities has increased rapidly, and many people are surprised to hear that city bees often produce more honey than bees in the countryside.

script.speaker: A
script.text: There are two main reasons for this. The first is variety. Parks, gardens and even balconies provide flowers throughout the season, whereas farmland may offer a single crop for only a few weeks. The second is temperature. Cities are warmer, so bees can begin collecting food earlier in the spring.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Let me give you some figures. In summer, a typical hive contains around fifty thousand bees. An individual worker bee lives for only about six weeks. In a good location, one hive can produce an average of twenty kilograms of honey a year.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Of course, there are challenges. Neighbours may worry about stings, so hives in cities are usually placed on rooftops, at least three metres above the ground, or behind a tall fence.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Another problem is competition. If there are too many hives in one area, the bees compete for nectar, and wild bees can suffer. Experts therefore recommend no more than about five hives per square kilometre.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Finally, people sometimes ask whether city honey is safe. It is regularly tested for pollution, and the results show that it is generally safe to eat. Thank you for listening.

listening.title: Listening mini-test 17: How we measure time (lecture)
listening.context: Vaqtni o‘lchash tarixi haqida ma’ruza (C1 daraja, IELTS Part 4 uslubida).

script.speaker: A
script.text: Today I want to look at how societies have measured time, and in particular at why accurate timekeeping became so important.

script.speaker: A
script.text: The earliest methods relied on the sky. Sundials, which use the shadow cast by the sun, were widely used in the ancient world. Their obvious limitation was that they were useless at night and on cloudy days.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Water clocks offered a partial solution. They measured time by the steady flow of water from one container to another, and some were remarkably sophisticated. However, the rate of flow changed with temperature, so their accuracy was limited.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Mechanical clocks appeared in Europe around the end of the thirteenth century, often in church towers. Interestingly, the first ones had no faces at all; they simply rang a bell to mark the hours.

script.speaker: A
script.text: A major improvement came in the seventeenth century with the pendulum, which made clocks far more accurate. But a pendulum does not work well on a moving ship, and this created a serious problem for navigation, because sailors needed accurate time to calculate their longitude, that is, their east–west position.

script.speaker: A
script.text: The solution was the marine chronometer, a clock designed to keep accurate time despite the movement of the sea and changes in temperature. It is no exaggeration to say that it made long ocean voyages much safer.

script.speaker: A
script.text: The next turning point was the railway. Before trains, each town kept its own local time, based on the position of the sun. That made timetables extremely confusing, so railway companies pushed for standard time across whole regions, and eventually time zones were agreed internationally.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Today, the most precise clocks are atomic clocks, which measure the vibrations of atoms. They are so accurate that they would lose less than a second over millions of years, and they are essential for satellite navigation systems.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's all from me. Enjoy your visit.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Hi, Daniel. Have you got a few minutes to talk about our presentation? It's only two weeks away now.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Sure, Emma. I've been reading about our topic, the four-day working week, and I think we've got plenty of material.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Good. I thought we could start with the trial that took place in Britain a few years ago. Most of the companies that took part decided to continue with the shorter week afterwards.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Yes, but I think we should be careful there. The companies chose to take part, so they were probably more enthusiastic than average. That might make the results look better than they would be in general.

script.speaker: C
script.text: That's a good point. We should mention it as a limitation.

script.speaker: D
script.text: What surprised me was that productivity didn't fall in most of the companies. I expected it to drop at least a little.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Me too. Apparently people cut down on long meetings and wasted time. One manager said meetings were reduced to thirty minutes.

script.speaker: D
script.text: And the staff reported less stress and better sleep. Although those results came from questionnaires, so they depend on what people said about themselves.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Right. Now, how should we divide the work? I'd be happy to do the background and the history of working hours.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Then I'll take the results of the trial. And maybe we can both do the conclusion together?

script.speaker: C
script.text: Fine. What about visuals? Our tutor said she wanted fewer slides with words and more charts.

script.speaker: D
script.text: I can make the charts. I'm better with spreadsheets than you are, I think.

script.speaker: C
script.text: That's true! I'll find a short video clip, then. Something from an interview with an employee, maybe. Not more than a minute, though.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Good idea. One thing I'm worried about is the question time at the end. Some people are bound to ask whether this would work in hospitals or schools.

script.speaker: C
script.text: We should prepare an answer to that. The trial was mainly in offices, so we can say the evidence for other sectors is still limited.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Agreed. When shall we practise?

script.speaker: C
script.text: How about next Wednesday afternoon in the library? We could book one of the study rooms.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Wednesday's fine, but the library rooms are always busy. Let's use the empty classroom on the second floor instead.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Perfect. I'll send you my part by Monday so you can read it first.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good morning. Today I'm going to talk about honeybees, and in particular about how they communicate. For a long time, people wondered how bees that had found a good source of food were able to direct other bees to it. The answer came from the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch, who studied bees for many years and later received a Nobel Prize for his work.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Von Frisch discovered that a bee returning to the hive performs a kind of dance on the surface of the honeycomb. When the food is close to the hive, the bee moves in small circles. This is called the round dance, and it simply tells the other bees that food is nearby.

script.speaker: A
script.text: When the food is further away, the bee performs what is known as the waggle dance. It runs forward in a straight line while shaking its body from side to side, then circles back and repeats the movement. The direction of the straight run shows the direction of the food in relation to the sun, and the length of the waggle tells the other bees the distance they need to fly.

script.speaker: A
script.text: What is remarkable is that the hive is usually dark, so the other bees cannot see the dance clearly. Instead, they follow the dancer closely and pick up the information through touch and vibration. They also learn the smell of the flowers from the dancer's body.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Of course, not every scientist accepted these findings at first. Some argued that bees simply followed the scent of the food. It was only later, when researchers used radar to track individual bees, that it became clear that the bees really did fly in the direction indicated by the dance.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Why does this matter today? Bees are responsible for pollinating a large proportion of the crops we eat, and in many regions bee populations have declined. Several causes have been suggested, including disease, the loss of wild flowers and the use of certain chemicals on farms.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Understanding how bees communicate can help farmers and planners. For example, if we know how far bees are prepared to fly, we can decide where to plant strips of flowers so that bees can reach them easily. In some cities, people are now encouraged to plant flowers on balconies and roofs.

script.speaker: A
script.text: In our next lecture, we'll look at how bees choose a new home when a colony becomes too large, a process in which, interestingly, the dance also plays a central role.

script.text: One. Excuse me, does this bus go to the airport?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Not this one, I'm afraid. You need the number forty-two. It leaves from the stop across the road every twenty minutes.

script.speaker: D

script.text: Three. Hi, I'm calling about my order. It was supposed to arrive yesterday, but nothing came.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Welcome to the Riverside Summer Festival. Here is some information to help you enjoy your day. The festival runs from ten in the morning until eleven at night. The main stage is in the centre of the park, and the first concert begins at two o'clock.

script.speaker: B
script.text: If you're interested in food, the market is next to the lake, where you can try dishes from more than twenty countries. Please remember that the festival is plastic-free, so bring your own bottle. Water is free at the fountains near each entrance.

script.speaker: B
script.text: For families, there's a children's area beside the north gate, with games and face painting. Children under twelve must be with an adult at all times. If you lose your group, go to the information tent, which is the large blue tent next to the main stage.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Finally, the festival ends with fireworks over the lake at ten thirty. The last buses back to the city centre leave at eleven fifteen, so please plan your journey home.

script.speaker: C
script.text: So, Bek, we need to choose a topic for our group project in economics. Any ideas?

script.speaker: D
script.text: I was thinking about small family businesses in our city. My uncle runs a bakery, so we could interview him.

script.speaker: C
script.text: That's a nice idea, but our teacher said the project should include data, not only interviews. Could we get numbers from your uncle?

script.speaker: D
script.text: He keeps records of his sales, and I think he'd share them if we don't publish his name.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Good. We could compare his sales before and after he started selling online. That would be interesting.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Agreed. He started online orders about two years ago. He says it was difficult at first because he had to learn to take good photos of the bread.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Ha! How about the presentation? I'm not very confident speaking in front of the class.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Then you could prepare the charts, and I'll present. But you should say at least one part, because the teacher gives marks to each person.

script.speaker: C
script.text: OK, I'll present the conclusion. That's the shortest part. When is the deadline again?

script.speaker: D
script.text: The twentieth of May. Let's aim to finish a week earlier, so we have time to practise.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Today on 'Working Lives' I'm talking to Daniel, who left his job in a bank to become a mountain guide. Daniel, why did you make such a big change?

script.speaker: D
script.text: Honestly, I was bored. The salary was good, but I spent all day in an office looking at numbers. At weekends I always went hiking, and one day I realised I was only really happy on Saturdays and Sundays.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Was it difficult to start?

script.speaker: D
script.text: Very. I needed a qualification, which took almost a year, and during that time I had almost no income. My family was worried, especially my father, who thought I was making a mistake.

script.speaker: A
script.text: And now?

script.speaker: D
script.text: Now he comes on some of my tours! He's changed his mind completely.

script.speaker: A
script.text: What's the hardest part of the job?

script.speaker: D
script.text: The weather. You have to make decisions quickly. If a storm is coming, you must turn back, even if the group is disappointed. Safety always comes first.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Do you earn as much as before?

script.speaker: D
script.text: No, less, maybe half in a bad year. But I spend less too, and I'm much healthier.

script.speaker: A
script.text: What advice would you give to people who want to change careers?

script.speaker: D
script.text: Try the new work part-time first, if you can. I guided small groups at weekends for a year before I left the bank. That way I knew I really enjoyed it.

script.speaker: A
script.text: In today's lecture I want to look at the history of tea, one of the most widely drunk beverages in the world. Tea originated in China, where it was first used as a medicine before it became an everyday drink.

script.speaker: A
script.text: From China, tea spread to Japan, where a formal tea ceremony developed, and later along trade routes to Central Asia, India and Europe. In Central Asia, tea became an important part of hospitality: offering tea to a guest is still a sign of respect.

script.speaker: A
script.text: In Europe, tea arrived in the seventeenth century. At first it was very expensive, so only wealthy families could afford it. It was often kept in locked boxes to prevent servants from taking it.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Over time, prices fell, largely because of large plantations established in India and later in Sri Lanka. By the nineteenth century, tea had become a drink for all social classes in Britain.

script.speaker: A
script.text: The way tea is prepared varies a great deal. In some countries it is served with milk, in others with sugar, lemon or even salt. Green tea, which is not fermented, remains especially popular in East Asia and in parts of Central Asia.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Next week we'll discuss coffee, and compare how the two drinks influenced trade and social life.
